solution.brief: Sets up a Wasp stochastic aggregation workflow where basic parts with geometry, connection directions, and custom attributes are assembled using generated rules, with results previewed and exported via file update.
solution.principle:
Related insight: Related insight: Tutorial 06 builds on the foundational single-part aggregation workflow established in tutorial 01 (wasp_01_basic_aggregation). The core 5-step pattern — define geometry, create connections, build WaspPart, set Rules, run Stochastic Aggregation — is a prerequisite for understanding the attribute and export extensions introduced here. Learners new to Wasp should complete the tutorial 01 basic workflow before engaging with custom attributes and file export.

Related insight: Related insight: Tutorial 05 (wasp_05_collider), which directly precedes tutorial 06, introduces collider and containment as growth-control features — Wasp collision detection against boundary BRep geometry constrains the aggregation within a defined volume. Tutorial 06 builds on a workflow that already includes this containment capability; learners should understand that spatial boundary constraints (tutorial 05) are a prerequisite concept alongside basic aggregation before engaging with the attribute and export extensions introduced in tutorial 06.

Related insight: Related insight: The wasp_06_multi_part pattern identifies the central architectural feature of tutorial 06 as multi-part aggregation — combining multiple distinct part types, each with their own connection geometry and configuration, in a single aggregation run. This is separate from (but co-present with) the custom attributes and export features. When working with multiple part types, each part's connection indices are independent and must be tracked separately; cross-part rules must explicitly reference the correct part name and connection index for each part type.

Related insight: Related insight: Tutorial 07 (wasp_07) is the direct successor to tutorial 06 — it advances beyond the multi-part aggregation, custom attributes, and file export features introduced here into more complex aggregation techniques. Tutorial 06 is the prerequisite for understanding the intermediate-to-advanced aggregation patterns explored in tutorial 07.

Related insight: Related insight: The same foundational setup used here — two part types with directional connections and custom attributes — can be paired with a graph-grammar aggregation engine instead of stochastic aggregation (as shown in wasp_graph_grammar_aggregation_setup). The part-definition and connection-configuration steps are identical; only the aggregation component differs. This makes the basic aggregation workflow a direct prerequisite for both stochastic and graph-grammar aggregation approaches.

intents: create a stochastic aggregation with Wasp
set up Wasp basic part with attributes
use Wasp to aggregate geometry with connection rules
build a Wasp assembly with custom attributes

evolution_history.changes: Tutorial 06 had empty context and was missing beginner/prerequisite framing. The new pattern explicitly establishes tutorial 01 as the foundational entry point, which tutorial 06 extends with attributes and export. Adding this lineage context and prerequisite tags helps learners understand the tutorial sequence.

Tutorial 06 is the direct successor to tutorial 05. Tutorial 06's context should reflect that tutorial 05 introduces collider/containment, not just basic aggregation, so learners understand the full scope of what precedes tutorial 06.

wasp_basic_aggregation_06 captured the attributes/export angle of tutorial 06 but underemphasized the multi-part connection configuration aspect. The new pattern provides complementary framing; adding this context and tags gives a complete picture of tutorial 06's scope.
wasp_07 directly follows tutorial 06 in the learning sequence; the tutorial 06 pattern should reference its successor just as tutorial 05 patterns reference tutorial 06.

The new pattern uses the same part-definition, connection, and attribute setup as this neighbor but substitutes graph-grammar for stochastic aggregation. Noting this distinction helps learners understand that the foundational workflow generalizes across aggregation engines.
